text: In Horseshoe Canyon, in southeastern Utah, a long sandstone wall called the Great Gallery is covered with painted figures. The life-size figures are tapered, with no arms or legs, but many have detailed designs. They were painted long ago by people who hunted and gathered their food, but no one knows their names.
more: Hikers reach the Great Gallery on a long walk, up to seven miles round trip.

text: High on a cliff in Capitol Reef National Park, a small stone storehouse still stands, and hikers can see it from a trail. The Fremont people built small granaries like it to store food and seed. The Fremont grew corn, beans and squash.
more: Fremont granaries like this sit on ledges and in cracks of the sandstone cliffs in Utah's canyons.

text: The word Utah comes from the Ute people. The Ute lived in the mountains and valleys of this land and moved with the seasons, hunting, fishing and gathering. Spanish travelers wrote their name as Yuta, and English speakers later turned it into Utah.
more: The Ute call themselves Nuche, which means the People.

text: The Goshute lived in the dry western desert near the Great Salt Lake, where water is scarce. They moved with the seasons to find food and water. They gathered pine nuts, seeds and roots, and they hunted rabbits.
more: In autumn, families went to the mountains to harvest pine nuts from the piñon pines, then stored them for winter.

text: In the red-rock country of southeastern Utah live the Navajo, who call themselves Diné. Monument Valley, with its tall sandstone buttes, sits on the border of Utah and Arizona inside the Navajo Nation. Navajo weavers are famous for rugs woven on upright looms.
more: A rug can take months to weave.

text: Utah is home to eight federally recognized tribes. They include the Ute, Paiute, Goshute, Northwestern Shoshone and Navajo peoples. They have their own governments, languages and ceremonies, and they are living in Utah today.
more: Many of the names on a Utah map began as words from these languages.

text: In July 1776, two Spanish friars, Domínguez and Escalante, left Santa Fe to find a route to California. They never reached it. They wandered through Utah, kept a daily diary, and came home after about 1,700 miles (2,700 km) in five months.
more: When winter closed in, they cast lots to decide whether to keep going. The lots said to go home.

text: On their way, the friars came down into a valley with a big freshwater lake, now called Utah Lake. The people there, called the Timpanogots, fished the lake, and they traded dried fish to the friars. Escalante's diary describes the valley.
more: The friars were the first Europeans known to visit the valley.

text: Late in 1824 or early in 1825, a fur trapper tasted the water of a huge lake and found it salty. He thought he had found an arm of the ocean. Most accounts name Jim Bridger, though some name another trapper. The lake was the Great Salt Lake.
more: Later trappers went all the way around the lake and found no outlet to the sea.

text: Each summer, trappers met at a rendezvous to trade beaver furs for supplies. Bear Lake, on the Utah and Idaho border, hosted the rendezvous in 1827 and 1828. A thousand or more trappers and Native Americans gathered there, and their campfires looked like a lighted city.
more: Besides trading, the rendezvous was a time of games and celebration.

text: In 1827, trapper Jedediah Smith and two companions crossed Utah's western desert on their way back from California. The lack of water and game made the trip very hard. Smith went on to the 1827 rendezvous at Bear Lake.
more: Smith may have been the first non-Native traveler to cross that desert.

text: In the 1840s, the explorer John C. Frémont mapped much of this region. He found that its rivers, such as the Humboldt, never reach any ocean. They end in lakes or sink into the sand. He named the region the Great Basin.
more: Water that falls in the Great Basin never flows to the sea.

text: The Great Salt Lake is so salty that swimmers float like corks. In some parts it is several times saltier than the ocean. No fish can live in it, but brine shrimp and brine flies thrive there, and the flies number in the billions.
more: Millions of migrating birds stop to feed on them.

text: No river flows out of the Great Salt Lake. Rivers flow in, bringing a little salt each day, but water can leave only by rising into the air. The water evaporates and the salt stays behind. That is why the lake stays salty.
more: Rain and snow can make the lake rise, and dry years make it shrink.

text: A railroad causeway built of rock divides the lake in two. The south arm gets fresh river water. The north arm does not, so it is much saltier, and salt-loving microbes turn its water pink or red.
more: From the air the two arms are two different colors.

text: West of the lake lie the Bonneville Salt Flats, a flat white plain of hard salt. It is so smooth that people have raced cars there to set land speed records since 1914.
more: The salt crust is less than an inch thick in places and about six feet thick in others.

text: The Uinta Mountains are the largest mountain range in the lower 48 states that runs east to west. Utah's tallest peak, Kings Peak, rises there to 13,528 feet (4,123 m).
more: The Uinta Mountains stretch across northeastern Utah.

text: Utah is one of the driest states in the country. On average it gets only a little over a foot of rain and snow a year. But the mountains catch heavy winter snow, and the melting snow runs down in streams. Most of Utah's water begins as mountain snow.
more: That is why Utahns watch the snowpack all winter long.

text: On July 24, 1847, Brigham Young reached the Salt Lake Valley. He had been sick with a fever, so the main company came in two days before him. Years later, a pioneer named Wilford Woodruff remembered him saying, "This is the right place."
more: July 24 is still a state holiday in Utah. It is called Pioneer Day.

text: The pioneers were members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, looking for a place of their own. The first company was small: about 150 people and 73 wagons. They left Winter Quarters, in what is now Nebraska, in April and traveled more than 1,000 miles (1,600 km).
more: The trip took more than three months.

text: To count the miles, Orson Pratt and William Clayton designed a roadometer, and Appleton Harmon built it. It was a wooden device on a wagon wheel, with gears that counted the turns of the wheel. Clayton wrote the distances in a guidebook.
more: It took 360 turns of the wheel to make one mile. Later pioneers used the guidebook, with the miles written down between landmarks.

text: When the pioneers arrived, they went to work at once. They sent water from a nearby creek into ditches to water the dry ground. They planted their first potatoes and turnips in a field near what is now Third South and State Street.
more: The settlers shared the water as one community.

text: From 1856 to 1860, about 3,000 pioneers crossed the plains pushing and pulling handcarts, two-wheeled wooden carts. Handcarts cost much less than wagons and oxen. Eight of the ten companies arrived safely. Two arrived late in 1856 and were caught by early snow until rescuers reached them.
more: Rescue wagons were sent out from the valley with flour and other supplies.

text: In 1848, swarms of crickets began eating the settlers' crops. People fought them with fire and ditches, but nothing worked. Then flocks of California gulls came and ate the crickets. A monument to the seagulls stands in Salt Lake City today.
more: The California gull is now Utah's state bird. It was named in 1955.

text: Salt Lake City was laid out in a grid of big square blocks with very wide streets, 132 feet (40 m) from edge to edge. The plan came from the Plat of Zion, a city plan Joseph Smith wrote down years before. A story says the streets were wide so oxen could turn around, but nobody has found proof.
more: Each block is 660 feet (200 m) on a side.

text: Addresses in Salt Lake City count out from the middle of town. The corner of Main Street and South Temple is the zero point. Each 100 numbers is one block, so 400 South 300 West means four blocks south and three blocks west of that corner.
more: State Street is 100 East, one block east of Main Street.

text: The beehive became the symbol of Utah. Bees work together and keep busy, and the beehive stood for hard work and thrift. Utah is the Beehive State, its motto is Industry, and a beehive is on its seal.
more: The beehive was chosen as the emblem of the State of Deseret in 1848. Industry here means steady, hard work.

text: The Salt Lake Temple took 40 years to build, from 1853 to 1893. The granite-like stone came from Little Cottonwood Canyon, about 20 miles (32 km) away. At first, oxen pulled each block on a wagon, and one round trip took three to four days.
more: Later a railroad carried the stone.

text: In 1849 the settlers asked for a state called Deseret, a word from their scripture that means honeybee. In 1850, Congress made it a territory instead and gave it the name Utah, after the Ute people.
more: The Territory of Utah was much bigger than the state is today.

text: Within a few years settlers built dozens of towns, some hundreds of miles from Salt Lake City: Provo, Ogden, Manti, Cedar City. In 1861 families were called to the hot southwest corner to grow cotton. They built St. George, still known as Utah's Dixie.
more: Winters there are mild. The cotton never paid well enough, so farmers gave it up, but the town stayed.

text: On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in northern Utah, two railroads met. A golden spike was set in a special tie, and telegraph wires carried the news across the country in one word: "Done." The two steam engines stood nose to nose.
more: A trip across the country that once took months now took days.

text: About 10,000 Chinese workers built the Central Pacific line through mountains and desert. On April 28, 1869, in Utah, crews laid 10 miles of track in a single day. No crew has equaled that record since.
more: Central Pacific boss Charles Crocker wanted to beat the Union Pacific's record of 8.5 miles in a day.

text: In 1904, a railroad shortcut called the Lucin Cutoff opened across the Great Salt Lake. Trains rode on a wooden trestle nearly 12 miles (19 km) long, built on wooden piles driven into the lake bottom.
more: In 1959 a rock causeway replaced the trestle, and trains still cross the lake there.

text: Bingham Canyon Mine, near Salt Lake City, is a copper mine dug as a giant open pit. Open-pit mining began there in 1906. The pit is about 3,650 feet (1.1 km) deep and 2.75 miles (4.4 km) wide, and it is often called the deepest open-pit mine in the world.
more: Giant haul trucks have tires about 12 feet (3.7 m) tall.

text: Silver was found in the mountains near Park City in 1868, and a mining camp grew up. Miners dug tunnels deep into the mountains for silver ore. About a hundred years later, the same mountains held ski runs.
more: In the 1960s the old mining company started a ski area on its mountain.

text: In 1952, a prospector named Charlie Steen found a rich uranium deposit near Moab. Most uranium prospectors carried Geiger counters, but Steen did not own one. His find set off a rush, and Moab's population grew to five times its size.
more: A Geiger counter clicks faster near radioactive rock such as uranium.

text: On January 4, 1896, President Grover Cleveland proclaimed Utah the 45th state. Bells rang and whistles blew in Salt Lake City, and towns across Utah held parades.
more: Utah had asked to become a state many times before it got a yes.

text: On February 14, 1870, a young woman named Seraph Young cast her vote in Salt Lake City. She is usually counted as the first woman in the United States to vote under an equal-suffrage law.
more: Congress took the vote away in 1887, and Utah's new constitution gave it back in 1896.

text: Utah's state seal shows an eagle on a shield, the word Industry, a beehive, and sego lilies on both sides of the beehive. An American flag stands on each side. The sego lily is the state flower.
more: Pioneers dug up sego lily bulbs to eat when food ran short.

text: Utah has some unusual state symbols. The state bird is the California gull. The state animal is the Rocky Mountain elk. The state cooking pot is the Dutch oven. The state fossil is Allosaurus, a meat-eating dinosaur.
more: Utah named the Dutch oven in 1997 and Allosaurus in 1988.

text: Martha Hughes Cannon, a doctor, ran for the Utah state senate in 1896 against her own husband. She won. She became the first woman state senator in the United States.
more: She also introduced a bill to create a state board of health, and it passed.

text: In 1850, the Territory of Utah was much larger than the state is now. It stretched from California to the Rocky Mountains and included the land that became Nevada. Over the next years Congress cut off pieces to make other territories and states.
more: In 1868 the last big piece went to Wyoming Territory, and Utah took the shape it has today.

text: Utah has five national parks, called the Mighty Five: Zion, Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef, Arches and Canyonlands. Each one shows a different side of the red-rock desert.
more: Together they cover more than a thousand square miles of canyons and cliffs.

text: Bryce Canyon is full of hoodoos, tall thin spires of rock that stand in rows like a crowd. Bryce has the largest collection of hoodoos in the world.
more: Frost may help shape them: about 170 days a year, the temperature there goes both above and below freezing.

text: In Zion Canyon the Virgin River has carved a slot so narrow that hikers wade in the river itself. In the Narrows, the walls rise up to 1,000 feet (300 m), and in places the gap is only about 30 feet (9 m) wide.
more: After a storm upstream, the river can rise fast.

text: Delicate Arch stands alone, and the opening under it is 46 feet (14 m) high. A picture of it has been on Utah's license plates. Arches National Park holds more than 2,000 natural stone arches, the densest collection in the world.
more: Rain soaks into the rock and ice pries it apart, slowly shaping the arches.

text: In Dinosaur National Monument in northeastern Utah, a whole wall of rock is full of dinosaur bones, about 1,500 of them, left where they were found so visitors can see them. Earl Douglass found the first huge bones there in 1909.
more: There are a few places where visitors can touch real dinosaur bones.

text: In 2002, Salt Lake City hosted the Winter Olympics. Utah calls its snow the Greatest Snow on Earth, because it falls light and dry. Some mountain resorts get more than 500 inches (12.7 m) of snow in a year.
more: Alta, a ski area near Salt Lake City, averages about 546 inches (13.9 m) of snow a year.
